name: Dahlia
handling: Deadhead deep and often. Runs to frost, then cut to four inches and mulch.
idNote: Cultivar unknown. Worth naming if you ever want to reorder the same one.

care.feed: Hungry. A spade of compost at planting, then a low-nitrogen feed such as tomato food every two or three weeks through July and August. Stop feeding by the end of August so it hardens off before the wet.
care.deadhead: Every few days in season, and cut deep: follow the stem down to a pair of leaves or a side bud and cut there, not just the head off the top. Spent heads are pointed and conical, unopened buds are round and firm.
care.good: Fat round buds, thick stems and dark green leaves mean it is happy.
care.poor: Yellowing lower leaves with few buds means hungry or dry. Ragged holes overnight are earwigs or slugs. A white bloom on the leaves late in the season is mildew and is not worth treating.
care.endOfSeason: Frost blackens the foliage, usually mid-November. Cut the stalks to about four inches, cap the hollow stems so rain cannot funnel into the crown, and mulch over the top.
care.propagate: Divide the tubers in spring, not when you lift them: wait until the eyes are visible and swelling, then cut so every piece has an eye. A piece without an eye never grows. Buy new tubers in late winter, which is when the good ones sell out.

name: Gaillardia
handling: Deadhead relentlessly. Dies of wet feet here, never of cold, so keep the crown dry and open.

care.feed: None, ever. It comes from poor dry ground and feeding it makes it floppy and shorter-lived.
care.deadhead: Weekly through summer. Cut each spent seed globe back to a leaf or side shoot. It stops flowering once it decides it has made enough seed, so this is the one job that keeps it going.
care.good: Compact growth and continuous flowers.
care.poor: Flopping open with a dead patch in the middle means it is either overfed or coming to the end of its life. Blackened crown after a wet spell is rot.
care.endOfSeason: Cut to four to six inches after frost rather than to the ground, so water cannot sit in a hollow crown. Keep mulch off the centre. It dies of wet feet here, never of cold.
care.propagate: Short-lived by nature, so plan on replacing it rather than keeping it going. It divides badly. Leave a handful of seedheads standing each year and it seeds itself, or sow fresh in spring. Expect to lose one or two over a wet winter.

name: Scabiosa
handling: Deadhead. Will run into November here.

care.feed: Nothing beyond an inch of compost on the soil surface in spring.
care.deadhead: Weekly. Cut the spent stem right down to the base of the plant rather than snipping the head off, or you leave a forest of bare stalks.
care.good: Long clean stems and steady flowering into November.
care.poor: Fewer and smaller flowers each year means the clump wants dividing. Grey mould on the buds in autumn means it is too crowded.
care.endOfSeason: Leave a few seedheads for the birds and tidy the rest. Cut the whole thing back in spring, not autumn.
care.propagate: Divide in early spring every three years or so, which is also the fix when flowering thins out. It self-sows lightly if you leave a few seedheads.

name: Cosmos
handling: Deadhead. Let a few set seed to self-sow.

care.feed: None. Rich soil gives you a six-foot leafy plant with almost no flowers, which is the single most common cosmos mistake.
care.deadhead: Weekly. Cut back to a leaf pair. Like the dahlias, cutting deep gets you two stems where there was one.
care.good: Airy growth covered in flowers.
care.poor: Tall, leafy and barely flowering means soil too rich or not enough sun.
care.endOfSeason: An annual, so frost ends it. Let a few heads shed seed first, then pull the plants. It self-sows reliably.
care.propagate: Self-sows readily. Let a few heads shatter where you want them next year, or collect the dry seed and sow straight into the ground after the last frost. It resents transplanting.

name: Sunflower
handling: Leave heads for birds, or cut when the back turns brown. The side bed plants have powdery mildew: strip the worst leaves and bin them, and do not spray this late. Sunflowers belong in the open sunny beds like the driveway patch, not against a west wall.
idNote: The dark red one is likely 'Velvet Queen' or 'Chocolate', but that is a guess from colour alone.

care.feed: None in reasonable soil. They are less hungry than their size suggests.
care.deadhead: Single-stem types have one flower and nothing to deadhead. Branching types keep producing if you cut spent flowers back to a side shoot.
care.good: A stout upright stem with a big head means full sun.
care.poor: Thin stems leaning hard in one direction with small heads means it is reaching for light it is not getting. White powdery coating is mildew, caused by still air and dry roots rather than by anything you did.
care.endOfSeason: Annual. Leave the heads for the birds through autumn, or cut when the back of the head has turned brown and yellow if you want the seed. Pull the stems whenever they look done.
care.propagate: Save seed from the best heads once the backs are brown, dry them indoors a week, and sow directly in May. They do not transplant well. Note that seed from a hybrid will not come true to the parent.

name: Echinacea
handling: Leave seedheads standing all winter for goldfinches. Cut in March.

care.feed: None. It is a prairie plant and prefers lean soil.
care.deadhead: Optional, and mostly not worth it. Deadheading the first flush brings a few more flowers, but the seedheads are the point of this plant in autumn and winter.
care.good: Strong upright stems and plenty of flowers.
care.poor: Fewer, smaller flowers each year means the clump needs dividing, roughly every three or four years. Distorted green deformed flowers mean aster yellows, which has no cure: dig the plant out and bin it.
care.endOfSeason: Leave every stem standing through winter for the goldfinches, then cut to the ground in March.
care.propagate: Divide in early spring every three or four years, which is also what fixes declining flower size. Autumn division is risky here because the wet winter rots new roots. It also self-sows if you leave seedheads.

name: Echinacea
handling: Same as the purple. Leave standing, cut in March.
idNote: Definitely a white echinacea. Which cultivar is a guess, and it only matters for reordering.

care.feed: None, same as the purple.
care.deadhead: Optional, same as the purple.
care.good: Strong stems and steady flowering.
care.poor: Declining flower size means it wants dividing.
care.endOfSeason: Leave standing all winter. Cut in March.
care.propagate: Same as the purple: divide in early spring, every three or four years. Seedlings from a named white will often come up purple, so divide rather than sow if you want to keep the colour.

name: Gladiolus
handling: Spike off now, leaves stay until fully yellow. Overwinters in these beds already. Inspect each corm when lifting and spreading in fall.
idNote: Confirmed as present. See the crocosmia entry for whether every strap-leaved clump is actually a glad.

care.feed: A light balanced feed when the shoots are about six inches, and again as the flower spike shows. Nothing after flowering.
care.deadhead: Not deadheading exactly, but cut the whole flower spike off at its base once the last floret fades. Letting it set those green seed capsules costs you next year's corm size.
care.good: Upright spikes and firm fat corms when you lift them.
care.poor: Silvery streaking and browning on the leaves means thrips. Corms that come up rough, corky or sticky are infested and go in the bin, not the compost.
care.endOfSeason: Leave every leaf until it has gone completely yellow, because that is what feeds the corm. Then cut at ground level and lift, inspect and spread the corms.
care.propagate: This is the free-plants one. When you lift the corms in autumn, each has a cluster of tiny cormels around its base. Pick them off, store them dry over winter, and grow them on in a nursery corner. They reach flowering size in two or three years.

name: California poppy
handling: Self-sows freely. Leave it to do that.

care.feed: Never. Feeding it produces soft floppy growth and fewer flowers.
care.deadhead: Not needed. Deadheading extends flowering slightly, but the seed is how it returns.
care.good: Blue-grey foliage and masses of flowers on lean dry ground.
care.poor: Lush green floppy growth means the soil is too rich or too wet.
care.endOfSeason: Annual here. Let it seed itself, then pull the spent plants whenever they look tired.
care.propagate: Self-sows and needs nothing from you. Never dig it up and move it: it has a long taproot and will not survive transplanting. If you want it somewhere new, scatter seed there in autumn.

name: Shirley poppy
handling: Shake pods where you want them, then pull the plants. Will not transplant and resents spring sowing.

care.feed: Never.
care.deadhead: Not worth it. This one is grown for the seed as much as the flower.
care.good: Masses of thin wiry flowering stems.
care.poor: Rich soil gives leaves rather than flowers.
care.endOfSeason: Shake the ripe pods where you want next year's plants, then pull. It will not transplant and resents spring sowing, so the autumn seed drop is the whole game.
care.propagate: Autumn seed drop is the whole method. Shake ripe pods where you want next year's plants, and keep a pinch in an envelope as backup. It will not transplant and resents spring sowing.

name: Snapdragon
handling: Cut spent spikes, leave the plants. Often overwinters here and returns. Let a few spikes shatter if you want more.

care.feed: A light feed in spring is plenty.
care.deadhead: Cut a finished spike back to a leaf junction lower down the stem and it will send up new spikes. This is the difference between six weeks of flowers and four months.
care.good: New side spikes coming after each cut.
care.poor: Orange powdery pustules on the undersides of leaves are rust, which is common here. Remove the worst leaves and give it more air.
care.endOfSeason: Cut the spent spikes but leave the plants standing. They are hardy enough to overwinter in Seattle and often come back for a second year.
care.propagate: Self-sows if you let a few spikes shatter, and often overwinters as a plant here anyway. Sow fresh seed indoors in late winter if you want particular colours.

name: Oregano
handling: Shear a third off now and dry the leaves. Hard prune into old wood in spring, not in fall.

care.feed: None. Feeding it makes it lush and noticeably less flavourful.
care.deadhead: Shear the whole plant back by about a third after it flowers. That is the only cutting it wants in autumn.
care.good: Dense aromatic growth.
care.poor: A woody bare centre with growth only at the edges means it is due for a hard renewal prune.
care.endOfSeason: Leave it through winter. Hard prune into the old wood in spring, never in autumn.
care.propagate: Easiest by division in spring, or by layering: pin a low stem to the soil, it roots, and you cut it free. Semi-ripe cuttings in late summer also work.

name: Hardy geranium
handling: Shear to a few inches for fresh foliage and often a second flush of flowers.

care.feed: None.
care.deadhead: Not individual flowers. Shear the entire plant back to a few inches once the main flush is over. It looks brutal, and within two or three weeks you have a fresh mound of clean foliage and often a second lot of flowers.
care.good: A tidy dense mound.
care.poor: Flopping open with a bare middle and tired yellowing leaves is the signal that it wants that shear.
care.endOfSeason: Leave the fresh foliage through winter and tidy any dead growth in spring.
care.propagate: Divide in spring, every three or four years or whenever the middle goes bare. Big clumps come apart by hand or with two forks back to back.

name: Whorled spike plant
handling: Leave the seed spikes standing either way. Only veronica gives a second flush if you cut them now.
idNote: Roll the stem: square with four flat sides means agastache, round means veronica. Then count leaves at one joint: two facing each other is agastache, three or more radiating like spokes is Culver's root. Best guess from photos is Culver's root.

care.feed: Hold off until it is identified. Feeding the wrong thing at the wrong time is one of the few ways to actively harm a plant.
care.deadhead: Depends on what it turns out to be.
care.good: Nothing specific until it is named.
care.poor: Nothing specific until it is named.
care.endOfSeason: Leave it standing until it is identified. Cutting back is easy to do later and impossible to undo.
care.propagate: Depends on what it turns out to be. Whether you divide it, let it seed or buy more differs completely between the candidates, so leave it until the identification is settled.

name: Silver-grey dried mound
handling: Do not pull until identified. Squeeze a stem at the base: brittle and hollow means dead, flexible and green inside means alive.
idNote: A large mass of fine grey branching stems. Candidates are artemisia, lavender, statice, or simply a spent annual. Crush a stem and smell it, then photograph the base of the plant where it meets the soil, and whether it has a woody trunk or many soft stems.

care.poor: Nothing specific until it is named.

name: Small blue flowers
handling: Harmless either way. Identify before deciding whether it returns next year.
idNote: Tiny blue-purple flowers on thin wiry stems threading through Street Bed 1. Lobelia is a low sprawling annual with tiny fan-shaped flowers. Salvia stands upright with flowers in tiers up a spike. A close photo of a single flower settles it.

care.deadhead: Depends on what it turns out to be.

care.poor: Nothing specific until it is named.
care.endOfSeason: Leave it standing until it is identified. Cutting back is easy to do later and impossible to undo.
care.propagate: Depends on what it turns out to be. Whether you divide it, let it seed or buy more differs completely between the candidates, so leave it until the identification is settled.

name: Round-leaved plant
handling: If nasturtium, it is an annual, edible, and will self-sow.
idNote: Nasturtium leaves are round like small lily pads with the stem joining in the middle of the leaf rather than at the edge. That centre-join is the giveaway.

care.feed: Hold off until it is identified. Feeding the wrong thing at the wrong time is one of the few ways to actively harm a plant.
care.deadhead: Depends on what it turns out to be.
care.good: Nothing specific until it is named.
care.poor: Nothing specific until it is named.
care.endOfSeason: Leave it standing until it is identified. Cutting back is easy to do later and impossible to undo.
care.propagate: Depends on what it turns out to be. Whether you divide it, let it seed or buy more differs completely between the candidates, so leave it until the identification is settled.

name: Small white daisy
handling: If feverfew, it self-sows enthusiastically and you may want to limit it.
idNote: Small white daisies with yellow centres. Feverfew has divided, slightly yellow-green foliage and a strong bitter smell when crushed.

care.feed: Hold off until it is identified. Feeding the wrong thing at the wrong time is one of the few ways to actively harm a plant.
care.deadhead: Depends on what it turns out to be.
care.good: Nothing specific until it is named.
care.poor: Nothing specific until it is named.
care.endOfSeason: Leave it standing until it is identified. Cutting back is easy to do later and impossible to undo.
care.propagate: Depends on what it turns out to be. Whether you divide it, let it seed or buy more differs completely between the candidates, so leave it until the identification is settled.

name: Possible crocosmia
handling: If present, keep it separate when lifting. Crocosmia spreads by underground corm chains and will colonise a bed.
idNote: Out of bloom the two look nearly identical. Gladiolus leaves are thicker, stiffer and stand upright in a flat fan. Crocosmia leaves are thinner, more pleated and arch over. The real tell is underground: a gladiolus corm sits alone with small cormels around its base, while crocosmia forms a vertical chain of corms stacked on top of each other. You will see it when you lift them this fall.

care.feed: Hold off until it is identified. Feeding the wrong thing at the wrong time is one of the few ways to actively harm a plant.
care.deadhead: Depends on what it turns out to be.
care.good: Nothing specific until it is named.
care.poor: Nothing specific until it is named.
care.endOfSeason: Leave it standing until it is identified. Cutting back is easy to do later and impossible to undo.
care.propagate: Depends on what it turns out to be. Whether you divide it, let it seed or buy more differs completely between the candidates, so leave it until the identification is settled.

name: Strawberry
handling: Do not mow the foliage. Thin the mat to about one plant every six to eight inches, pinch off runners you do not want, and let a few root as replacements.
idNote: Confirmed as strawberries in the side bed. The remaining question is only which type: fruiting in late August points to everbearing or day-neutral rather than June-bearing, and that is what the care here assumes. A heavy single crop in June would mean the opposite.

care.feed: Feed matters here. A balanced feed after the first flush of fruit and again in midsummer. Top-dress with compost in spring, but keep it off the crowns, which rot if buried.
care.deadhead: Not deadheading. The equivalent job is runners: pinch off the ones you do not want so the plant puts its energy into fruit rather than into travelling.
care.good: Dark green leaves and steady fruit through the season.
care.poor: Pale leaves and small fruit means hungry or too crowded. Reddening leaves late in the season is usually age. Grey fuzz on the fruit is botrytis, which comes from damp still air.
care.endOfSeason: These are everbearing, so do not mow the foliage down: that advice is for June-bearing types and would cost you fruit. Pull dead leaves, thin the mat, and replace the oldest crowns every three or four years.
care.propagate: The runners are the renewal. Peg a few down into gaps in summer and they root by autumn, then cut them free from the parent. Replace the oldest crowns every three or four years: plants decline sharply after that, and a bed kept going indefinitely quietly stops fruiting.

name: Pole beans
handling: Keep picking, which is what keeps them producing. When finished, cut at soil level and leave the roots in the ground for the nitrogen in the nodules.

care.feed: None. They fix their own nitrogen, and feeding gives you a magnificent vine with very few beans.
care.deadhead: Picking is the deadheading, and with pole beans it is the whole game. Every pod left to swell and mature tells the vine it has reproduced and can stop. Pick every two or three days at the height of it, taking pods while they still snap.
care.good: Flowers and pods forming all the way up the strings rather than only at the bottom, and pods that snap cleanly instead of bending.
care.poor: Production stopping in late summer usually means picking fell behind rather than anything being wrong. Pods that are lumpy and stringy were left too long. On a west wall like this one, a slow start is normal: they want warm soil and this bed is shaded all morning.
care.endOfSeason: They carry on until frost or until the vine exhausts itself, usually well into September here. When done, cut the stems off at soil level rather than pulling, so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the ground. Take the strings down and clean the trellis so nothing overwinters on it.
care.propagate: Leave a few pods on the vine until they are papery and rattle, then shell and store the seed somewhere cool and dry. This only comes true from an open-pollinated variety, not an F1 hybrid. Sow fresh in May, direct into warm soil, and get the supports in before you sow rather than after.

name: Dark puckered greens
handling: All three are edible and all three can be picked leaf by leaf, so it is safe to harvest either way.
idNote: Growing low among the beans, deeply savoyed dark leaves. Chard has a thick white or coloured midrib and stalk. Beet has a reddish stalk and a swelling root at the base. Spinach has thin plain stalks and no swollen root. Look at the stalk colour and scrape the soil at the base.

care.feed: Hold off until it is identified. Feeding the wrong thing at the wrong time is one of the few ways to actively harm a plant.
care.deadhead: Depends on what it turns out to be.
care.good: Nothing specific until it is named.
care.poor: Nothing specific until it is named.
care.endOfSeason: Leave it standing until it is identified. Cutting back is easy to do later and impossible to undo.
care.propagate: Depends on what it turns out to be. Whether you divide it, let it seed or buy more differs completely between the candidates, so leave it until the identification is settled.

name: Low creeping ground cover
handling: Weed it out now either way, before it seeds or spreads further into the strawberry mat.
idNote: Small round leaves running along the soil between the strawberries. Chickweed is soft, shallow-rooted and pulls out in mats, and is a minor annual nuisance. Ground ivy has scalloped leaves, a square stem, a strong minty smell when crushed, and roots at every node, and it is a genuine long-term problem. Crush a leaf and roll the stem: this one is worth knowing.

care.feed: Hold off until it is identified. Feeding the wrong thing at the wrong time is one of the few ways to actively harm a plant.
care.deadhead: Depends on what it turns out to be.
care.good: Nothing specific until it is named.
care.poor: Nothing specific until it is named.
care.endOfSeason: Leave it standing until it is identified. Cutting back is easy to do later and impossible to undo.
care.propagate: Depends on what it turns out to be. Whether you divide it, let it seed or buy more differs completely between the candidates, so leave it until the identification is settled.

name: Rosemary
handling: Never cut into bare wood: rosemary does not resprout from it and the cut stays a hole forever. Trim only into green growth, and only in spring. The branches sprawling on the soil will root where they touch, which is free plants.

care.feed: Never. It wants poor sharp-draining soil, and feeding shortens its life.
care.deadhead: Nothing to deadhead. Trim only into green growth, and only in spring.
care.good: Aromatic dense green tips and new growth from the outer stems.
care.poor: A bare woody centre is normal ageing and cannot be pruned out. Blackened or grey stems after winter means it sat too wet.
care.endOfSeason: Nothing in autumn. Cutting a woody Mediterranean herb in autumn pushes soft growth that dies in the first cold snap, and cutting into bare wood leaves a permanent hole because it does not resprout from it.
care.propagate: Never by division, and never from an old woody stem. Take semi-ripe cuttings in late summer, which is roughly now, or layer a low branch by pinning it to the soil and cutting it free in spring once rooted. Since a bare-centred rosemary cannot be pruned back into shape, growing its replacement is the actual fix.

name: Sage
handling: Same rule as the rosemary. No fall pruning, no cutting into old wood, no mulch piled against the crown. Prune in spring once new growth shows.

care.feed: Never, same as the rosemary.
care.deadhead: Nothing to deadhead. Prune lightly into green growth in spring only.
care.good: Soft grey aromatic leaves and growth from the outer stems.
care.poor: Woody bare centre and sparse leaves means it is ageing out. Take cuttings rather than trying to cut it back into shape.
care.endOfSeason: Leave it entirely alone in autumn, and keep mulch and compost off the crown.
care.propagate: Same as rosemary: semi-ripe cuttings in late summer, or layering. It does not divide. A sage that has gone woody and sparse is replaced rather than rescued, so take the cuttings a year before you need them.

name: Shasta daisy
handling: Cut the spent stems down to the low green mound at the base. Divide every three years or so: the centre dies out and the flowering moves to the edges.

care.feed: An inch of compost in spring. Nothing else.
care.deadhead: Cut spent stems right down to the low mound of green leaves at the base. Doing it early enough sometimes brings a second smaller flush.
care.good: Strong stems that hold their flowers up without staking.
care.poor: Flopping and a dying centre with flowering pushed to the edges means it wants dividing, roughly every three years.
care.endOfSeason: Cut the flowered stems down and leave the basal rosette of leaves, which stays green through winter. Divide in early spring, not autumn: a division going into a wet Seattle winter on new roots is the one that rots.
care.propagate: Divide in early spring every three years. Discard the tired woody centre and replant the vigorous outer pieces. Do not divide in autumn here: new roots going into a wet winter are the ones that rot.

name: Bearded iris
handling: Late summer is the window for dividing. Cut the leaves back to a fan about six inches tall and replant the rhizomes shallow, with their backs showing above the soil. Burying them is the usual reason iris stops flowering.

care.feed: A low-nitrogen feed in early spring. Never manure or rich compost over the rhizome, which makes it rot.
care.deadhead: Snap spent flowers off as they go over, then cut the whole flower stalk down to the base once the last one has finished.
care.good: Fat firm rhizomes sitting at the soil surface with fans of clean leaves.
care.poor: A soft, smelly rhizome is rot and must be cut out. Brown streaks and spots on the leaves are leaf spot, which overwinters on old foliage. Plenty of leaves but no flowers almost always means the rhizomes are buried too deep or too congested.
care.endOfSeason: Cut the leaves back to a fan about six inches tall and clear every dead leaf away, since leaf spot overwinters on old foliage. Division happens in late summer, which is the window closing now, and the rhizomes go back in shallow with their backs showing above the soil.
care.propagate: Divide in late summer, six weeks or so after flowering, which is the window closing right now. Each piece needs a fan of leaves and some roots, and goes back in shallow with the rhizome top showing. Discard anything soft or hollow.

name: Blue-green upright plant
handling: If euphorbia, wear gloves. The milky sap burns skin and is genuinely bad in eyes, so identify it before cutting anything back.
idNote: Upright stems with blue-green leaves spiralling around them, back left of the bed. Snap a leaf off and watch the break, from a safe distance: milky white sap means euphorbia. Do not get the sap on your skin.

name: Volunteer seedling
variety: compound leaves, possibly ash or elder
handling: Pull or cut it while it is still small enough to pull. A tree seedling in a narrow bed becomes a much bigger job every year you leave it.
idNote: Woody, with leaves divided into several toothed leaflets along a central stalk. Ash and elder both self-sow readily in Seattle and both get large. Photograph a whole leaf flat, and check whether leaves come off the stem in opposite pairs.

name: Zinnia
handling: Cut-and-come-again: deadhead deep, back to a leaf junction rather than snipping the flower off, and it keeps producing until frost kills it outright. Very prone to powdery mildew here, so give it air and water the soil rather than the leaves.
idNote: Told to me rather than seen. The type matters only for seed saving: big dahlia-flowered kinds come fairly true, mixed bedding types scramble. A photo of one flower would settle it.

care.feed: A light feed monthly through summer is enough.
care.deadhead: Cut deep, back to a leaf junction rather than snipping the flower off. Zinnias are cut-and-come-again and this is what keeps them going to frost.
care.good: Compact plants covered in flowers.
care.poor: Tall floppy growth with few flowers means not enough sun. White powdery coating on the leaves is mildew, which zinnias are very prone to here: water the soil rather than the leaves and give them space.
care.endOfSeason: Frost kills them outright. Leave three or four heads to dry on the plant for seed, collect once brown and crisp, then pull.
care.propagate: Save seed from heads left to dry brown and crisp on the plant. The seeds are the arrowhead flakes at the base of each petal. Big dahlia-flowered types come fairly true; mixed bedding types scramble. Sow direct after the last frost, since zinnias hate root disturbance.

name: Wildflower mix
handling: Let most of it stand and shed seed, which is how a mix carries itself into next year. Pull anything that is clearly taking over before it seeds.
idNote: A mix is many species, and knowing which ones changes everything about how it is managed. If you still have the seed packet it lists them, which beats identifying them one by one. Failing that, photograph the three or four most numerous plants.

care.feed: None. Wildflower mixes are designed for poor soil and feeding them favours the coarse species over the pretty ones.
care.deadhead: Not practical across a whole patch, and not the point of it.
care.good: A good spread of different species flowering in succession.
care.poor: One or two vigorous species taking over is the usual failure. Pull those before they seed.
care.endOfSeason: Let most of it stand and shed seed, which is how the patch carries itself into next year. Clear it whenever it looks finished.
care.propagate: It carries itself by seeding, so leave most of it standing to shed. Oversow bare patches with fresh mix in autumn rather than spring, so the hardy species get their cold period.

name: Tulips
handling: Let the leaves die down fully after flowering, never cut them green: that is when next year's flower is made. Most tulips fade after a year or two in wet Pacific Northwest soil, so top up with fresh bulbs each autumn rather than expecting the display to hold.

care.feed: Bulb fertiliser or bonemeal worked in at planting, and a low-nitrogen feed as the shoots come through. Nothing once flowering is over.
care.deadhead: Take the spent flower head off so the plant does not waste energy setting seed, but leave the stem and every leaf.
care.good: Fat buds and broad healthy leaves.
care.poor: Leaves but no flower, which gardeners call blind, means the bulb is depleted, planted too shallow, or was too small to begin with.
care.endOfSeason: Leave the leaves until they have yellowed completely, then pull them away. Most tulips fade after a year or two in wet soil here, so the display is kept up by planting fresh bulbs each autumn rather than by the same ones returning.
care.propagate: Realistically, buy and replant rather than propagate. Most tulips fade after a year or two in wet soil here. You can lift and separate the offsets around the parent bulb, but they take years to reach flowering size and it is rarely worth it. Order in August and September, plant October into December.

name: Candytuft
handling: As close to no-work as a plant gets. Evergreen, smothers the ground so weeds cannot start, and needs only a light shear after flowering to stop it going bare in the middle.

care.feed: None.
care.deadhead: Shear the whole plant back by about a third straight after flowering. That single cut is the entire year's maintenance.
care.good: A dense evergreen mat that smothers weeds.
care.poor: A bare woody middle with flowers only around the edge means the annual shear has been missed a few years running.
care.endOfSeason: Nothing in autumn. It is evergreen and earns its place through winter.
care.propagate: Cuttings taken right after the post-flowering shear root easily. It also layers itself where stems touch soil, so you can often just lift a rooted piece in spring.

name: Aubrieta
handling: Shear it back by about a third right after it finishes flowering. That is the whole job for the year.
idNote: Purple cushions flowering with the candytuft and spilling over the wall. Aubrieta is the usual suspect, though a creeping phlox looks similar at a glance. Aubrieta leaves are small, grey-green and slightly hairy; phlox leaves are narrow and needle-like.

care.feed: None.
care.deadhead: Shear back hard right after flowering, by about a third. Leave it and it goes straggly and bare-centred.
care.good: A tight cushion covered in flower in April.
care.poor: Long bare trailing stems with a thin sparse centre means it needs that shear.
care.endOfSeason: Nothing in autumn.
care.propagate: Take cuttings from the trimmings when you shear it after flowering. It also self-layers, so rooted pieces can be lifted and moved in spring.

name: Sweet alyssum
handling: Leave it to seed itself, which it does reliably. No work at all.
idNote: White carpets through the upper bed. Sweet alyssum is the obvious call. Confirm by smell: it is strongly honey-scented, which nothing similar is.

care.feed: None.
care.deadhead: A light shear when it starts looking tired brings another flush, but it is genuinely optional.
care.good: Low mounds of scented white flower over a long season.
care.poor: Legginess and browning in the middle means it is coming to its end, which is normal for an annual.
care.endOfSeason: Let it set seed and it returns on its own. Pull spent plants whenever they look tired.
care.propagate: Self-sows generously and needs nothing. If you want it in a new spot, scatter seed there in spring.

name: Primroses
handling: Divide congested clumps after flowering every few years. Otherwise leave alone.
idNote: The low rosettes with bright flowers scattered through the spring display. Which primula type is worth knowing only if you want more of the same.

care.feed: An inch of compost around the crowns in spring.
care.deadhead: Pull spent flower stalks off at the base to keep it flowering longer.
care.good: Fresh green rosettes and early flowers.
care.poor: Crowded congested clumps flower less, which means divide after flowering. Ragged leaf edges are slugs or vine weevil.
care.endOfSeason: Leave the foliage alone. It is evergreen here and next year's crown is inside it.
care.propagate: Divide right after flowering, in May, every few years. Lift the clump, pull it apart into rosettes each with roots, and replant straight away. It self-sows too.

name: Violas and pansies
handling: Self-sow readily if you let a few set seed. Deadheading extends them but is optional.
idNote: Small faced flowers in mixed colours. Violas and pansies are near-identical in care, so the distinction barely matters here.

care.feed: A light feed occasionally, or none at all.
care.deadhead: Pinch spent flowers off between finger and thumb. It genuinely does prolong flowering, and it is a pleasant five-minute job rather than a chore.
care.good: Continuous flowering over months.
care.poor: Straggly stems and few flowers in high summer means heat, and they usually pick up again as it cools.
care.endOfSeason: Let some set seed and they return. Pull the tired ones.
care.propagate: Self-sows freely if you let some flowers set seed. Sow fresh seed in late summer for the strongest spring plants.

name: Periwinkle
handling: Superb at holding a wall and suppressing weeds, and it needs nothing from you. Keep it cut back off the bed edges: it roots wherever a stem touches soil.
idNote: Trailing mats with small blue star-shaped flowers over the wall face. Worth confirming, because both common vincas are listed as invasive in Washington and escape into wooded areas. It is fine held in a wall like this, but do not let clippings travel.

care.feed: None. Feeding a vigorous groundcover is asking for trouble.
care.deadhead: Nothing to deadhead.
care.good: Dense evergreen cover holding the wall and keeping weeds out.
care.poor: The failure mode is the opposite of struggling: it roots wherever a stem touches soil and will travel.
care.endOfSeason: Shear it back off the bed edges whenever it oversteps, at any time of year. Both common vincas are listed as invasive in Washington, so bag the clippings rather than composting them.
care.propagate: Propagates itself whether you want it to or not: every stem that touches soil roots. Lift rooted pieces any time of year to move it. The real job here is limiting it rather than increasing it, and clippings go in the bin rather than the compost.

name: Creeping thyme
handling: If thyme, it needs sun, sharp drainage and no feeding, and it is one of the lowest-effort plants you can own.
idNote: Low sprawling grey-green mats hanging down the wall. Crush a piece: thyme is unmistakably thyme. If there is no scent it is more likely a rockcress or a stonecrop.

care.feed: None, if it is thyme. It wants poor sharp-draining soil.
care.deadhead: Shear lightly after flowering.
care.good: Dense aromatic mats spilling over the wall.
care.poor: Woody bare patches and dieback in the middle usually means it has been sitting too wet.
care.endOfSeason: Nothing in autumn. Depends on the identification being right, so worth confirming before you cut anything.
care.propagate: Layers itself along the ground. Lift rooted sections in spring and replant. Division of an established mat works too, in spring.

name: Japanese maple
handling: Almost no maintenance. Do not prune in spring when it is running with sap; late summer or winter if it ever needs it. Note that it casts shade over part of the bed as it leafs out.

care.feed: None. A light mulch of compost over the root area in spring at most.
care.deadhead: Nothing to deadhead.
care.good: Clean well-coloured foliage and steady growth.
care.poor: Crisped brown leaf edges by August is scorch from too much sun or dry roots. A whole branch wilting and dying back in summer can be verticillium wilt, which is serious and worth getting looked at.
care.endOfSeason: Leave it. If it ever needs pruning, do it in late summer or deep winter, never in spring when it is running with sap and will bleed heavily.
care.propagate: Not practical at home. Named varieties are grafted, and seedlings do not come true. This is a buy-one, keep-it-forever plant.

name: Daffodils
handling: Unlike the tulips these do return and multiply here. Leave the foliage until it yellows. Divide congested clumps every few years.
idNote: Strap-shaped foliage among the tulips with a few yellow flowers. Confirm next spring when they bloom.

care.feed: Bonemeal at planting, and a low-nitrogen feed after flowering while the leaves are still green.
care.deadhead: Snap the spent flower head off so it does not set seed, and leave every leaf.
care.good: Clumps that get thicker and flower more each year, which is the difference between these and the tulips.
care.poor: Leaves but no flowers means the clump is congested and wants lifting and dividing.
care.endOfSeason: Leave the leaves until they yellow completely, six weeks or so after flowering. Never knot or cut them green.
care.propagate: These are the ones that genuinely multiply for you. Lift and divide congested clumps once the foliage has died back in June or July, separate the bulbs, and replant in autumn. A clump that has gone all leaves and no flowers is telling you it is time.
